analysis.one_liner: Caps the federal share of crop insurance premiums and ends direct farm subsidy payments.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the House Agriculture Committee and its subcommittee in spring 2013 and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would cut three kinds of federal farm spending. It would cap the government's share of crop insurance premiums at 70%, so farmers would pay more out of pocket. It would repeal the 'direct payments' program, which sends annual checks to producers of major commodities and peanuts regardless of crop prices or harvest outcomes. And it would bar the Agriculture Secretary from sending money to a Brazilian cotton institute set up under a trade dispute settlement. The bill died in committee without ever coming to a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers, who currently fund roughly the bulk of crop insurance premiums and annual direct payments to commodity producers; the bill would return that money to the Treasury rather than send it to agricultural producers and insurers.

how_it_helps.text: Caps the federal share of any crop insurance premium at 70%, ending cases where taxpayers cover more of a farmer's premium than that [S2] [S3].

Repeals the direct payments program for producers of covered commodities and peanuts, ending annual checks paid regardless of crop prices or yields, after honoring payments for the 2013 crop year [S2] [S3].
Prohibits the Secretary of Agriculture, directly or through the Commodity Credit Corporation, from making payments to the Brazilian Cotton Institute [S2] [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Producers of corn, wheat, cotton, rice, peanuts, and other covered commodities would lose direct payments and pay a larger share of crop insurance premiums. Crop insurance companies and agents would face a smaller, subsidy-fed market. Brazilian cotton interests would lose payments the U.S. had been making under the trade settlement.

drawbacks.text: Farmers and their groups argue that subsidized crop insurance is the main safety net for catastrophic losses like drought, and that raising farmers' premium share or shrinking participation could leave disaster risks uninsured, with losses then made up through ad-hoc disaster bills [S2].

The payments to the Brazilian Cotton Institute were not simple foreign aid: they flowed from the U.S. settlement of a World Trade Organization case over American cotton subsidies, so cutting them off could invite retaliation against U.S. exports [S2].

The bill would cut payments unilaterally and immediately after the 2013 crop year, with no transition or replacement program, which even fiscal critics of farm subsidies generally paired with new risk-management tools when reform eventually passed.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The savings are real and go to all taxpayers, but they are modest in the scheme of federal spending, and the strongest objection is fair: direct payments were pure price-and-production-independent checks, yet crop insurance subsidies also serve a genuine risk-management purpose. A designed reform would have phased changes in and paired them with a risk-management program; this bill simply ends the payments and caps the premium share. The Brazilian Cotton Institute ban, on its own, carries more diplomatic risk than budgetary gain.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Agriculture Committee and then to a subcommittee, and no one ever scheduled it for a hearing or a vote, so it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Ron Kind introduced the bill on April 18, 2013, for himself and Rep. Earl Blumenauer [S1] [S3].
The same day, the House referred it to the Committee on Agriculture [S5].
On May 3, 2013, it was referred to the Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management [S5].
No further action appears in the record: the bill never received a hearing, markup, floor vote, or Senate companion action before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015 [S1] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Commodity producers and the crop insurance industry, who kept uncapped federal premium subsidies and direct payments through the 2013 crop year and faced no committee action on the caps or repeal; by the time the Congress ended, no reform along these lines had moved from this bill.

for.name: Rep. Ron Kind
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to cap crop insurance premium subsidies, repeal direct payments, and ban payments to the Brazilian Cotton Institute.

for.name: Rep. Earl Blumenauer
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill as an original cosponsor.

against.name: House Committee on Agriculture
against.role: Committee of jurisdiction; chaired by Rep. Frank Lucas (R-OK)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and never scheduled it for a hearing or markup; it then went to a subcommittee and no further action was taken before the Congress ended.

against.name: House Subcommittee on General Farm Commodities and Risk Management
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after its May 3, 2013 referral and took no action on it.

against.name: Farm commodity producers and the crop insurance industry
against.role: Recipients of direct payments and federally subsidized crop insurance
against.what_they_did: Opposed capping the federal premium share and repealing direct payments during this period; the Agriculture Committee, whose members represent farm districts, took no action on the bill.

sides.party_line_note: Only two Democrats are on the record for the bill (Kind and Blumenauer) and no Republicans cosponsored; there were no votes, so no partisan breakdown exists, though the Agriculture Committee that buried it was chaired by a Republican.

industries.note: The federal government pays most of the premium on crop insurance policies, which delivers guaranteed premium volume to private insurers and agents. Capping the federal share at 70% would have shrunk that taxpayer-fed market.

industries.industry: Producers of covered commodities and peanuts (corn, wheat, cotton, rice, soybeans, peanuts, and others)
industries.note: Direct payments were annual checks based on historical production, paid whether prices were high or low. Repeal would have ended roughly $5 billion a year in payments funded by taxpayers, and the 70% premium cap would have raised farmers' out-of-pocket insurance costs.
The U.S. had been making payments to a Brazilian cotton institute under the settlement of a WTO dispute over U.S. cotton subsidies. The bill would have cut that stream off entirely.
